nodes.label: Screenshot titled 'Order-level CAPI Breakdown': a dark-themed dashboard table listing individual Meta CAPI (Conversions API) events per order, with columns Order, Customer, Value, Quality (Tracked/Untracked badge), Est. EMQ, Lead, Checkout, Purchase, and Signals. Subtitle reads 'Every order sent to Meta — click any row to open the order. EMQ is estimated based on signals available.' Untracked orders show a red 'Untracked' badge, Est. EMQ of 2.5, and only an 'Email' signal. Tracked orders show a green 'Tracked' badge and Est. EMQ of 5.5 with signals Email, FBP, IP, UA; the highest row shows Est. EMQ 7.5 with signals Email, FBC, FBP, IP, UA, UTM. All visible rows have a checkmark in the Purchase column (Lead and Checkout columns empty/dash).

Insight (inferred from chart pattern): Meta's estimated Event Match Quality (EMQ) score scales with the number/type of match signals sent per order — orders with only an Email signal (client-side/untracked) plateau around EMQ 2.5, while server-side CAPI-tracked orders that add browser/device identifiers (FBP, IP, UA) reach EMQ 5.5, and adding click-id and campaign signals (FBC, UTM) pushes EMQ to 7.5. This demonstrates the blog post's likely core argument: enriching Meta Conversions API payloads with more first-party match signals directly raises EMQ and thus ad tracking/attribution quality. Likely data source: a custom or third-party CAPI monitoring/analytics dashboard built for or by the blog's business, showing real (anonymized/blurred) order and customer data.
